en: Itivuttaka 55: Tikanipāta, Paṭhamavagga Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard: “Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person who is like a stone pillar, the person who is like a tree stump, and the person who is like a lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a stone pillar? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with mind obsessed by sensual desire, overwhelmed by sensual desire; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual desire. That sensual desire increases in him, and he passes away with a mind obsessed by sensual desire. He dwells with mind obsessed by ill will, overwhelmed by ill will; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. That ill will increases in him, and he passes away with a mind obsessed by ill will.

He dwells with mind obsessed by sloth and torpor, overwhelmed by sloth and torpor; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sloth and torpor. That sloth and torpor increase in him, and he passes away with a mind obsessed by sloth and torpor. He dwells with mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse, overwhelmed by restlessness and remorse; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen restlessness and remorse. That restlessness and remorse increase in him, and he passes away with a mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse. He dwells with mind obsessed by doubt, overwhelmed by doubt; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen doubt. That doubt increases in him, and he passes away with a mind obsessed by doubt. Just as a stone pillar, sunk in the earth, would be blown about by the four winds—by the wind from the east, the west, the north, and the south—and would not shake, tremble, or quiver; even so, monks, this person is called ‘one like a stone pillar. And how, monks, is one a person like a tree stump? Here, monks, a certain person has abandoned the five lower fetters and become a non-returner, one who will not return to this world. Having passed away from here, he will attain final nibbāna in that very realm. He is incapable of falling back into a state of misery, or into the lower realms, or into the abyss. Just as a tree stump, standing firm in the ground, would not be blown about by the four winds—by the wind from the east, the west, the north, and the south—and would not shake, tremble, or quiver; even so, monks, this person is called ‘one like a tree stump. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having transcended the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, attained the cessation of perception and feeling, and remains therein. By the destruction of the taints, he has realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it, he abides therein. Just as a blue, red, or white lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and stands unsoiled by the water; even so, monks, this person is called ‘one like a lotus flower. These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus was it said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Farer rose from his seat and went to his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the monks: “Friends, friends! “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. The Venerable Ānanda said this: “Friends, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and gone to his dwelling after speaking thus: ‘Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world… These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Now, friends, it is fitting for us to go to the Blessed One and inquire about the meaning of this statement. “Yes, friend,” those monks replied to the Venerable Ānanda. Then the Venerable Ānanda, together with a number of monks, went to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: “Venerable sir, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and gone to his dwelling after speaking thus: ‘Monks, there are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world… These, monks, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Now, venerable sir, it is fitting for us to go to the Blessed One and inquire about the meaning of this statement. “Ānanda, it is well that you understood this matter in such a way. Ānanda, it is exactly as you have understood it. There are these three kinds of persons found existing in the world. What three? The person like a stone pillar, the person like a tree stump, and the person like a lotus flower. And how, Ānanda, is one a person like a stone pillar? [As before]... Even so, Ānanda, this person is called ‘one like a stone pillar. And how, Ānanda, is one a person like a tree stump? [As before]... Even so, Ānanda, this person is called ‘one like a tree stump. And how, Ānanda, is one a person like a lotus flower? [As before]... Even so, Ānanda, this person is called ‘one like a lotus flower. These, Ānanda, are the three kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the Venerable Ānanda and those monks rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said.
The Second Discourse on Searches.
This was said by the Blessed One; thus have I heard:
"Bhikkhus, there are these three searches."
“What three?
The search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence, and the search for the holy life.
These, monks, are the three searches.”
The Blessed One spoke this matter.
Regarding this, it is said:
“The search for sensual pleasures, the search for existence,”
The quest for the holy life,
along with clinging to truth—
these are the standpoints of views, these lofty piles.
For one who is detached from all lust,
liberated through the destruction of craving,
seeking has been relinquished.
The bases for views have been uprooted;
with the destruction of all searches,
the bhikkhu is free from longing and beyond doubt.
This matter too was spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
The sixth [discourse].
